title: She remembers, and he comes
hookLine: Satyavati tells Bhishma about her firstborn and calls Vyasa with a thought: why Hindus repeat God's name
carry: smarana: remembering god is itself devotion
last: I WILL NOT GIVE UP TRUTH.

cards: Bhishma has refused her, but he doesn't leave her empty-handed. He tells old stories of lines carried on in hard times, when a learned man was invited to father children for a house that had none.

Find such a man, he says. And Satyavati, the text says, smiles, and her voice falters with shyness. Then the queen mother tells her stepson something she has carried since before she ever saw a palace.

teach.b: She tells him about the boat: the sage Parashara, the mist on the Yamuna, the son born on an island.
That son, she says, is Dvaipayana, the great sage people call Vyasa, and when he left he promised to come whenever she thought of him. If you agree, I'll think of him now. Bhishma agrees.

teach.h: SHE THINKS OF HIM. HE COMES.
teach.b: Satyavati thinks of her son, and that's all it takes. Vyasa appears at once, the text says. He bows to his mother; she weeps and holds him, and tells him plainly what the house needs.

Look back over the week: a vow and a boon, a baby in a fish, a boat and a fragrance, a proud son fallen, Amba's choice, Bhishma's no. And the one door left open is the one she opened herself, years ago, on a river.
In Hindu devotion, remembering isn't small. It has a name: smarana. When the boy Prahlada lists the ways to love God in the Bhagavata Purana, remembering comes third, right after hearing and singing.
That's why so many Hindus keep a name of God going through the day: Ram, Ram while cooking, beads in the morning, Krishna's name before sleep.

It's called naam smaran, remembering the name, or japa when it's counted on a mala. Many teachers say the idea isn't that God is far away and must be summoned. Remembering turns you toward the one who was near all along.
Satyavati thinks, and her son comes. A devotee remembers, and the holy is there.

how: Many Hindus keep a mala of 108 beads for japa, repeating a name of God or a mantra once on each bead; others simply keep a name like 'Ram' going under their breath through the day.

o: the queen who sends Bhishma to find a sage
the sage's wife who calls Parashara back
the queen mother who calls her firstborn, Vyasa

p: comes when she thinks of him

s: in bhakti, remembering God is only a warm-up
Prahlada's list of nine ways to love God puts remembering third.
Vyasa came the moment Satyavati thought of him
just as he'd promised when he left the island.
Satyavati told her secret to no one
she told Bhishma, smiling and shy, and he agreed.

games.q: a friend sees your Nani's prayer beads and asks what they're for. what fits?
o: japa: repeating a name of God, bead by bead. remembering is itself devotion.
a good-luck charm against bad dreams.
a way to count the prayers she owes.
games.why: smarana, remembering, is one of the nine ways of bhakti. Satyavati thought of her son and he came; a devotee remembers, and God is near.

practice: Many Hindus repeat a name of God, often on a mala of a hundred and eight beads. Choose a name that's dear to you: Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, or Om. Say it softly, once with each slow breath, for a couple of minutes.
If you don't pray, choose a word you love, like shanti, peace, and do the same. When your mind wanders, that's fine; remembering again is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Satyavati. The fisherman's daughter who became queen mother of the Kurus, and called her son home by remembering him.

orig.note: Sanskrit smaraṇa, remembering: one of the nine ways of devotion in Prahlada's list.

carryVoice: Your line: smarana, remembering God is itself devotion. Next, the birth of the cousins. Day seven hundred twenty-one, done.
